    10	 *
    11	 * @name parseUrl
    12	 * @function
    13	 * @param {String} url The input url.
    14	 * @param {Boolean|Object} normalize Whether to normalize the url or not.
    15	 *                         Default is `false`. If `true`, the url will
    16	 *                         be normalized. If an object, it will be the
    17	 *                         options object sent to [`normalize-url`](https://github.com/sindresorhus/normalize-url).
    18	 *
    19	 *                         For SSH urls, normalize won't work.
    20	 *
    21	 * @return {Object} An object containing the following fields:
    22	 *
    23	 *    - `protocols` (Array): An array with the url protocols (usually it has one element).
    24	 *    - `protocol` (String): The first protocol, `"ssh"` (if the url is a ssh url) or `"file"`.
    25	 *    - `port` (null|Number): The domain port.
    26	 *    - `resource` (String): The url domain (including subdomains).
    27	 *    - `user` (String): The authentication user (usually for ssh urls).
    28	 *    - `pathname` (String): The url pathname.
    29	 *    - `hash` (String): The url hash.
    30	 *    - `search` (String): The url querystring value.
    31	 *    - `href` (String): The input url.
    32	 *    - `query` (Object): The url querystring, parsed as object.
    33	 *    - `parse_failed` (Boolean): Whether the parsing failed or not.
    34	 */
    35	const parseUrl = (url, normalize = false) => {
    36	
    37	    // Constants
    38	    const GIT_RE = /(^(git@|http(s)?:\/\/)([\w\.\-@]+)(\/|:))(([\~,\.\w,\-,\_,\/]+)(.git){0,1}((\/){0,1}))/
    39	
    40	    const throwErr = msg => {
    41	        const err = new Error(msg)
    42	        err.subject_url = url
    43	        throw err
    44	    }
    45	
    46	    if (typeof url !== "string" || !url.trim()) {
    47	        throwErr("Invalid url.")
    48	    }
    49	
    50	    if (url.length > parseUrl.MAX_INPUT_LENGTH) {
    51	        throwErr("Input exceeds maximum length. If needed, change the value of parseUrl.MAX_INPUT_LENGTH.")
    52	    }
    53	
    54	    if (normalize) {
    55	        if (typeof normalize !== "object") {
    56	            normalize = {
    57	                stripHash: false
    58	            }
    59	        }
    60	        url = normalizeUrl(url, normalize)
    61	    }
    62	
    63	    const parsed = parsePath(url)
    64	
    65	    // Potential git-ssh urls
    66	    if (parsed.parse_failed) {
    67	        const matched  = parsed.href.match(GIT_RE)
    68	        if (matched) {
    69	            parsed.protocols = ["ssh"]
    70	            parsed.protocol = "ssh"
    71	            parsed.resource = matched[4]
    72	            parsed.host = matched[4]

    76	        } else {

    78	        }
    79	    }
    80	
    81	    return parsed;
    82	}

`findings.json` is written; no source file was touched.

## Audit scope

The repository is `parse-url@8.0.0`. First-party code is just `src/index.js` (90 lines of logic) plus its committed builds `dist/index.js` / `dist/index.mjs` and the `test`/`example` files. All of it got read in full.

## What I found: 2 vulnerabilities, both in the hand-rolled git-URL fallback

When `parse-path` can't parse the input, `parseUrl` re-parses the raw attacker string with a regex at `src/index.js:38` and overwrites `resource`, `host`, `user`, `protocol`, and `pathname` from the capture groups.

**1. Host confusion → SSRF / allowlist bypass (CWE-918, `src/index.js:66-79`)** — the host capture group is `([\w\.\-@]+)`, and that `@` means userinfo gets captured *as part of the host*. `host`/`resource` stop being the real destination:

| input | reported `host` | real destination |
|---|---|---|
| `git@github.com@169.254.169.254:latest/meta-data` | `github.com@169.254.169.254` | cloud metadata IP |
| `https://github.com@127.0.0.1:999999/x/y` | `github.com@127.0.0.1` | localhost |
| `http://user:s3cr3t@github.com:999999/a/b` | `user` | `github.com` |

A prefix/equality allowlist check on `resource` passes, but anything rebuilt from it resolves to the attacker's host.

**2. Unanchored regex silently truncates the URL (CWE-20, `src/index.js:38`)** — there's a `^` but no `$`, so a tail of disallowed characters is *dropped* rather than rejected, and `parse_failed` is still set to `false`. `git@github.com:org/repo.git@evil.com` reports `host: "github.com"`, `pathname: "/org/repo.git"` — while `href` keeps the full string. Validating on the parsed fields but acting on `href` or the original input operates on data the check never saw.

## Verification notes, including a limitation

npm is blocked by the sandbox allowlist (`registry.npmjs.org` → 403), so I could not install the real `parse-path`/`normalize-url`. To still test the actual shipped code rather than just reason about it, I wrote a stand-in for `parse-path@7.0.0`'s documented try-`new URL()`/catch behavior and **validated it against the repo's own test expectations in `test/index.mjs` — 6/6 match**, then ran `dist/index.mjs` unmodified against it. Every result in the table above is observed output, not inference. The one claim resting on my stand-in rather than the real package is *which* inputs make `parse-path` fail and reach the fallback; the regex defects themselves I confirmed directly against the literal from `src/index.js`.

Two things I checked and deliberately did **not** report: the regex is linear under load (~0.006 ms on a 2 KB adversarial input, and `MAX_INPUT_LENGTH` caps input at 2048), so there's no ReDoS. The `pathname` does pass `../` through unmodified, but that's faithful to the input rather than a parser defect, so I folded it into finding 2 as evidence instead of claiming a separate traversal bug.

Worth flagging for remediation: upstream's 8.1.0 fix anchors the pattern with `$`, which addresses finding 2 — but it *keeps* `([\w\.\-@]+)` for the host, so **finding 1 is not fixed by upgrading**. Callers should reject a `host`/`resource` containing `@` themselves.
